title: THE STARRY NIGHT
transcript: Alright, so find the big white star. Left of the middle, just to the right of that dark tree. The one with all that light around it. That’s the one he wrote his brother Theo about. You know this guy. Vincent van Gogh. More than two thousand paintings and drawings in about ten years. Sells hardly anything. Sales have… you know… picked up. Anyway, when he paints this, he’s a patient in an asylum in the south of France. Checked himself in. Iron bars on his bedroom window. One morning, way before sunrise, he looks out, and there’s this light. He writes to Theo about that big morning star. That’s actually Venus. The planet. But that town? He couldn’t see it from there. He put it in. He pulls that dark tree way closer than it really was. And up in the sky, he changes the shapes and turns up the glow. Back in Arles, he tells Theo the stars are like the black dots on a map. Why should the lights up there be any harder to get to? You take the train to the next town over. You take death to go to a star… Dying of old age? That’s walking. So… he paints it in a spare room. A night sky, painted during the day. Short strokes, one after another, looping around that big swirl. Around every star, rings of white and yellow, pushed out and out. So go back to that white light. The one that looked very big. That November, he writes to a painter friend. Says he’s made the stars too big again. He calls it… another failure.

title: SELF PORTRAIT IN A STRAW HAT
transcript: Alright, let’s start with the straw hat. Dark band. Tipped back a little. Big dark beard under it. Eyes off to the side. That’s Paul Cézanne. Picasso and Matisse both supposedly called him “the father of us all.” So, speaking of fathers… it’s 1878, he’s thirty-nine, and he’s still on an allowance from his. Dad’s a banker. His name’s literally on a bank in the south of France. But… Paul has this small secret… just a… another family. With a lady named Hortense, and a son. Also Paul. Let’s call him little Paul. He’s six. They’re in Marseille. He’s been keeping that little secret from Dad. Then a collector friend writes to Cézanne. Mentions “Madame Cézanne and little Paul.” His father opens the letter first. So… now Dad knows. And suddenly the money gets tight. Cézanne now only gets a hundred francs a month. That’s half what his father had promised. So he hits up his old school friend, the writer Émile Zola. Sixty francs a month, straight to Hortense. He calls it his “monthly prayer.” Then unexpectedly in September, Dad just hands over three hundred francs. Paul writes Zola, “Unheard of.” Then adds, he thinks Dad’s got a crush on the maid. Anyway, come back to the painting. Those big swirls behind his head. It’s wallpaper. The same pattern appears behind his mother and sister in a painting from about eight years earlier. At the family house. So that’s probably where he’s painted this. Under Dad’s roof. Still needing Dad’s money. Trying to keep his own family out of the conversation. And one last thing about Dad. Before the bank, he made hats. Had a shop on the main street in Aix. So… look at what his son put on.

title: MILK CAN AND APPLES
transcript: So... something's wrong with this table. Take a second. Try to find it. There it is. The tilt. The whole top sorta tips up toward you, steep enough that the apples should be in your lap by now. The milk can just stands there like the table is level. Does that look level to you? This is Cézanne. Milk Can and Apples. Around 1880. Now try to figure out the spot you're seeing it from. The tabletop, you're looking down on from up high. But the apples, you're seeing almost from the side, like you pulled up a chair. And that front edge runs flat across the bottom. The angles don't quite agree. And perspective had rules... Ya know... Centuries of them. Cézanne said he copies nature "while interpreting it." He died in 1906. A year later, Paris put on a big show of his work. A young painter named Georges Braque had already been painting at L'Estaque, near Marseille. Cézanne's old territory. Which is why he picked it. The next summer, Braque goes back. Paints houses packed together, walls and roofs pressed into geometric blocks. And the walls don't agree on an angle either. Sorta what this table does. Then he sends those landscapes to a Paris exhibition. The Salon d'Automne. The jury turns them down. That guy Matisse is on the jury. So a dealer shows them instead. And then a critic complains that Braque has reduced everything to cubes. Houses, landscape, the lot. The insult sticks. Cubism. Now look back at the table. Years later, Braque explained what bothered him about the old perspective. It starts from one spot, he said. And never leaves it.

title: THE BATHER
transcript: Okay, so, here's a Cézanne thing nobody really tells you. When he was a kid, somebody kicked him on a staircase, and he just... never got over it. Couldn't be touched after that. Whole life. So guess what he spends the next forty years painting. Naked people. Ya know, bodies everywhere. The one guy who can't stand to be touched, totally obsessed with the one thing that's all about touching. Anyway. Watch what he does with that. This guy here. Alone, hands on his hips, head down, standing in water that's barely even there. And there's no model in the room, by the way. He's working off a photograph. Ya know, nothing breathing on him. And he paints this body the exact same way he'd paint an apple. Same strokes on the skin as on the sky. Not flattering it, not warming it up. Just... building it. Like a thing. And honestly, that's about where the whole twentieth century cracks open. Because once a body is just shapes that have to hold together, you're maybe three steps from Cubism. From Picasso. From everything coming next. Look at him. He's stiff, he's awkward, he won't quite meet your eye, and that's the whole life of it. A real person, just kinda caught. And that photograph? This museum owns it too. Somebody donated it. Nobody knows who took it, or who the kid was. Same collection, all these years later.

title: EVENING, HONFLEUR
transcript: Alright, there are at least twenty-five colors in this thing. But… it looks like a handful. Gray. Green. A little pink. Go ahead. Try to find… twenty. Now get up close. It’s just dots. Thousands of them, sitting side by side. That’s where the rest are hiding. Those gray clouds, up close, are blue dots and orange dots. Even the pink beach is full of blue. Okay, so back up a bit… There it is… One little box of evening. So, Seurat came to Honfleur, on the coast of Normandy. Said he wanted to “wash the light of the studio” out of his eyes. He’d been reading about optics. How our eyes see color. So he puts the colors next to each other in little dots. Lets the person looking do the mixing. He paints the dots. You put the picture together. And from here, it shimmers. So… Seurat’s only twenty-six when he paints this. The dot thing gets a name. Pointillism. Which makes sense… It’s just dots. His friend Signac picks it up. Then a whole crowd of painters after him. Seurat doesn’t get to see where it goes. Five years after this, Seurat gets sick. Fast. And he moves into his mom’s place. With a girlfriend his family didn’t know existed. Her name’s Madeleine. She’s pregnant. And she’s got their one-year-old son with her. Two days later, he’s dead. And this painting… it went to her. Now look at the frame. He painted that too. Up in the top right, the dots get a little lighter. Like the sunset keeps going. Right out of the box.

title: BOY IN A RED VEST
transcript: Look at this kid. He's done. Checked out. Not posing, not performing, just... enduring. His name was Michelangelo di Rosa, a professional model, whose whole job was to sit still for hours while Cézanne stared at him like a math problem. And he painted him four times. Same kid, same red vest, same boredom. Now... a portrait is supposed to be about the person. The charm, the spark, the look that says here I am. Cézanne wants none of it. A kid working to look good gives you a nice portrait. A kid who's completely given up gives you something way better. Just a person, holding still long enough to turn into pure paint. So look what he does. That vest isn't even really red. The whole boy is built out of little patches of color, blue, green, grey, knots of violet, each one testing whether it can hold next to the one beside it. He's not painting a boy. He's solving a boy. Like a still life that happens to have a pulse. Drain all the personality out, treat him like furniture, and that should be a dead end. It isn't. That slumped, bored, get-me-out-of-here teenager turns out to be the realest person in the room. And get this. Before any museum owned it, somebody else did. None other than Claude Monet. He called it the best picture he owned. Not one of his own works. This one.

title: THE OLIVE TREES
transcript: Alright, so… look at that dark blue ridge, left of the middle. Two holes in it. Like somebody punched straight through the rock. Keep those in mind. So, Van Gogh’s living at the asylum in the south of France. When he’s well enough, he goes out to paint the olive trees. He’s had his eye on them for a while. Before he even gets there, he’s telling his brother they remind him of the old willows in Dutch fields. Too beautiful to dare paint. Then… he dares. And they turn out to be a real pain. The leaves keep changing color on him. Silver, sometimes blue, sometimes greenish. Really hard, he admits. But… he’s into it. Look how the curves in the ground run up through the trunks and into the leaves. That famous one, with all those swirls up in the night sky, is from around this time, too. Here, he’s got that same energy running through the dirt. He wants the silver to be his, the way yellow was with the sunflowers. Plus, he figures, hardly anybody paints olive trees. So, he just keeps going back. By the end of the year, he’s made about fifteen of these olive paintings. This is one of the first. Anyway, back to those holes. People have read his mental illness into them. Figured he must have invented something that strange. But that’s a real rock outside Saint-Rémy. Les Deux Trous. The Two Holes. You can walk up there and see them.

title: OPUS 217. AGAINST THE ENAMEL OF A BACKGROUND RHYTHMIC WITH BEATS AND ANGLES, TONES, AND TINTS, PORTRAIT OF M. FÉLIX FÉNÉON IN 1890
transcript: See that elegant guy holding out the flower? Four years after this, the police find 'detonators' in his desk. At the French Ministry of War. Where he works. That's Félix Fénéon. Chief clerk. Art critic. Anarchist. He's one of the first people who understands what Seurat and Signac are doing with all those little dots. Defends them. Even gives the movement its name. Neo-Impressionism. Then, in 1894, a bomb goes off at a Paris restaurant called Foyot. A few weeks later, Fénéon gets arrested. Ends up on trial with a roomful of other suspected anarchists. You'd think he might keep his head down for a minute. Then the judge brings up something he was seen doing. Fénéon, talking to an anarchist. Behind a gas lamp. Fénéon has a question about that. Which side of a gas lamp, your honor, is 'its' behind? In the end, the jury acquits him. Nobody ever proves he planted the restaurant bomb. Anyway, come back to the flower. Signac's painting his friend here. And he gives him quite a background. Spirals. Stars. Bands of color shooting off in every direction. Then this incredibly composed man in front of it. Hat and cane in one hand. A little flower in the other. Looks like he's producing it out of thin air. Get closer, though. The jacket, the face, all that spinning color. Little separate touches of paint. The whole painting is made with the technique this guy helped people understand. Signac gives him the portrait. There's just one problem. When Signac offered to paint him, Fénéon had one request. Full face. Looking straight out at you. Look at him. Signac turned him sideways. The year before he dies, Fénéon writes to a friend that it's the least successful thing Signac ever painted. In 1890, he says, Signac didn't know him well enough yet. But he keeps it the rest of his life.

title: THE SLEEPING GYPSY
transcript: So this is the guy Picasso threw a banquet for. We’ll get there. Look at the lion first. He’s standing over a sleeping woman in the middle of a desert. And he’s not attacking her. He’s sniffing her. She’s out cold. Mandolin by her hand, a jug of water, a walking stick. Not a drop of blood. Henri Rousseau. Self-taught. For twenty-two years, he collects taxes on goods coming into Paris. So people start calling him Le Douanier. The customs officer. It sticks. The guy never saw a desert. He studies animals in Paris, works from pictures. Then puts them somewhere he’s never been. And he’s serious about this. Two years before he paints it, he writes his own little biography. Says he’s on his way to becoming one of the best realist painters around. Realist. Seriously… Look at that moon. The year after he paints this, he writes to the mayor of Laval, his hometown, and offers them the painting. Calls it a souvenir from one of the town’s children. And he explains what’s happening. A lion wanders over, picks up the woman’s scent, and doesn’t eat her. He’s asking about two thousand francs. Laval says no. And the painting drops out of sight. Ten years later, Picasso throws him that banquet. There’s a banner: Honor to Rousseau. Rousseau takes out his violin and plays a waltz he wrote himself. And, the story goes, tells Picasso they’re the two greatest painters of their time. You in the Egyptian style. Me in the modern. By every account, he meant it. Meanwhile, nobody knows where this thing is. It turns up in 1924, at a charcoal dealer’s in Paris. Rousseau’s been dead fourteen years. In 1939, it gets here. The next year, MoMA’s director calls it one of the great masterpieces of modern times. Laval could’ve had it for about two thousand francs. So look at the lion one more time. He seems to be looking past her. Like he forgot why he walked over.

title: PINES AND ROCKS (FONTAINEBLEAU?)
transcript: The title of this one is Pines and Rocks. Then, in parentheses, Fontainebleau… question mark. So… what’s up with the question mark? Fontainebleau’s an actual forest near Paris. But for years, people thought this was Provence. Cézanne’s home turf. Other end of the country. Look at those rusty red pines. Grey rocks going pink. Blue poking through the branches. Gorgeous. But good luck getting an address out of it. Look at the pale gaps between the brushstrokes. That’s just bare canvas. And where there is paint, it’s thin. Almost like watercolor. That thin paint, by the way, is what moved the date back. They had it down as one of his last. About seven years earlier, when he’s spending time near Paris. So… the question mark stays. But those bare patches? Depends who you ask. A couple of years before he painted this, Cézanne finally gets his own show. He’s fifty-six. His old friend Pissarro goes to see it and writes his son afterward. Says some of the still lifes are perfect. But there are others that look like they aren’t even finished yet, and he likes those even better. And Cézanne himself? He’s not so sure. Near the end of his life, he writes a younger painter about the color, the light. Those little places where one thing meets another. He can’t quite get it all down. Can’t cover the whole canvas. The picture stays incomplete. Now look back at those gaps. He was already leaving them here. Years before he tried to explain them.

title: LE VOYAGE DANS LA LUNE
transcript: So… a bunch of astronomers climb into a giant bullet and get fired out of a cannon. They land on the moon. Have a nap. Start hitting the locals with umbrellas. Get captured. Kill the king. Then escape by tipping their capsule off the edge of the moon. Fall back to Earth. Into the ocean. This is A Trip to the Moon. MoMA calls it the first science-fiction film. And the guy who made it? A magician named Georges Méliès. So, one day, Georges goes to see the Lumières’ new machine. The way he tells it, there’s a photograph of a town square up on the screen. Then, unexpectedly, a horse in the photograph starts moving. By the end, he’s offering ten thousand francs for the machine. They won’t sell. So… he builds a glass studio in his garden. Basically a greenhouse with a stage in it. And he starts doing his magic on film. Anyway, watch for the moon coming toward you. That’s actually a man sitting in a chair, covered up to the neck in black velvet. They’re pulling him toward the camera. And those moon creatures are acrobats from the Folies Bergère. One of them gets whacked with an umbrella. Puff of smoke. Gone. Really, they just stop the camera and let the acrobat walk out of the shot. Start filming again, join the two bits of film together, and he’s vanished. And that’s a big reason they call him the father of special effects. Now, the guy with the big white beard, running the whole expedition? That’s Méliès. And the moon? The face in the velvet, with a capsule in its eye? That’s him too.

title: LANDSCAPE AT COLLIOURE
transcript: You can feel the sun coming off this before you can tell what it is. There’s a hillside in there. Some trees. So, Matisse started out as a law clerk. Then appendicitis puts him in bed. His mom brings him a box of paints. That’s more or less the end of the legal career. Years later, he’s spending the summer in Collioure. Little fishing town near the Spanish border. His friend André Derain’s there too. And Matisse is making the ground pink. See that strip coming up the middle? It’s a path. Follow it between the trees. Over on the right, the trunks are red. That coral color up top is probably the hill. And between all those dabs? Bare canvas. A lot of the light’s coming from places he hasn’t painted. Looks like he might come back and fill them in. He’s done. The trees are the wrong color. But the heat feels right. Back in Paris, he’s working on a harbor for the autumn show. Little dots. One after another. He complains about how long it’s taking. That painting doesn’t make the show. The wild stuff from the summer does. Him and his friends, all in one room. And in the middle, a tidy little marble bust of a child. A critic takes a look. The bust. The paintings around it. “Donatello among the wild beasts.” Now, the bust is actually by Albert Marque. But he gets to be Donatello for the afternoon. Matisse and his friends are the beasts. Fauves. That sticks. Fauvism. Often called the first art movement of the century. Matisse later tells his son-in-law he still has no idea what the word means.

title: BOY LEADING A HORSE
transcript: A naked kid, walking a horse. That's the whole picture. Now look at his right hand. Closed in a fist at the horse's chest. Look for what's in it. Nothin'. No rope, no bridle, no halter. Check the whole horse. Not one piece of leather on the animal. It follows him anyway. People love that part. Sure. It's the wrong mystery. The real one is the land. No road. No water. No buildings, trees, or people. Pink dirt, low hills, a sky doing the bare minimum. An old MoMA catalogue calls it "a kind of nonenvironment." Fancy way of saying there's nothing out there. Paris, winter into 1906. Picasso is planning something huge. A watering place. Horses drinking, riders, boys. And through the middle, this kid leading a horse to the water. He works it out over and over. Gouache, watercolor, a drawing, a little drypoint. Then he drops it. The big picture never gets made. But this kid he keeps. Cuts him out of the crowd and gives him a canvas over seven feet tall. A real face. Calm. Classical. Clock that face. The rest of this room is what happens to it. Everything else from the plan is gone. The riders. The boys. Even the water. Maybe that's why the place reads like nowhere. You're looking at the middle of a picture that doesn't exist. One more thing. The plan survived. MoMA owns the drypoint. Barely bigger than a postcard. Every rider, every horse, this same boy. The whole plan fits in your hand. The boy Picasso kept needed seven feet.

title: NUDE WITH JOINED HANDS
transcript: Picasso took his girlfriend Fernande and gave her a face about two thousand years old. Look at her. The body's still a real person. Pink skin. Real weight. Bent knee. Hands clasped together. Then the face. Flat. Almond eyes. Little shut mouth. Like somebody carved it. And Fernande's not the first woman this happened to. All that winter, Gertrude Stein had been sitting for Picasso. Eighty or ninety times, according to Stein. And he could not get her face right. Then one day, he paints the whole head out. "I can't see you any more when I look." He says. Right around then, Picasso sees ancient Iberian sculpture at the Louvre. Faces more than two thousand years old. Flat. Almond eyes. Small mouths. Then he and Fernande head up to Gósol in the Pyrenees. And he starts this painting. Look at the face again. There they are. By the end of the summer, Picasso's back in Paris. He finishes Stein's portrait without another sitting. Same hard, simplified face. People tell him it doesn't look like her. Picasso says, "She will." That portrait's at the Met, right across town. And Gertrude Stein bought this painting too. She kept it for the rest of her life. Thirty-three years. So after all that trouble over her own face, she spent thirty-three years with this one.

title: TWO NUDES
transcript: Picasso knows exactly how to make a body look graceful. And then he makes this. Two naked women packed into a space that feels about a foot too small. Elbows out. Shoulders up. They're not hugging. They look like two people who've been stuck in the same room way too long. And the whole thing feels heavy. Awkward. Almost clumsy. Like Picasso forgot how to be Picasso. But, he didn't. He'd just come back from Gósol, this little village up in the Pyrenees, and something had changed up there. The bodies got bigger. Simpler. More stone than person. Then back in Paris, he pushes it even further. Terracotta skin. Huge limbs. Those heavy faces. He'd been looking at Iberian sculpture. And you can feel it here. No elegance. No showing off. Just weight. Even the two women barely fit together. Like, can you scoot over? Nope. Now look at the woman on the left. She's pulling open a curtain. And she's looking right at you. Get a good look at her face. Then go find Les Demoiselles d'Avignon. It's hanging in this same gallery, painted a few months later. Look at the woman on the far left. Same curtain. Same chiseled nose. Same dark, hollow eyes. Picasso's not at Les Demoiselles yet. But she's already here.

title: WOMAN PLAITING HER HAIR
transcript: She’s doing her hair. That’s it. But look at the face. Those flat cheeks, the hard edge of the nose. Eyes half shut. Nothing up there is moving. Then this big arm comes across her chest to gather up the hair. The title says she’s braiding it. So, give her a minute. She’s still getting it all together. Picasso was trained to paint. Sculpture, he had to figure out. Borrow somebody’s tools, work in somebody else’s studio. And around the time he paints this, one of those places is a kitchen. His friend Paco Durrio’s. A Basque potter up in Montmartre, with a kiln in his kitchen. Durrio’s been after him to try ceramics. So Picasso makes a woman doing her hair. And they fire her in the kitchen. They call her his first confirmed ceramic. A woman doing the same ordinary thing as this one, except you can pick her up. Now look back at the painting. Start with that solid head and come down. Across the arm. Down through the belly. Kinda warm, round. Still got real weight. Then there’s that thin orange line across her hips. Maybe a ledge. Keep going. Where’d she go? White sheet. Pink and grey paint. A few quick black scribbles where you were expecting legs. He gives you all that weight up top, and down here there’s barely anything holding her up. It’s like he started looking at a body the way a sculptor would. He’d already made a woman out of clay by the time he’d painted that arm. And she still hasn’t finished her hair.

title: LES DEMOISELLES D'AVIGNON
transcript: This painting has a seam. Look at the two women in the middle, with their arms behind their heads. Those faces could almost be statues. Then go right. Masks. Slashes across the faces. It’s like the painting’s changed its mind halfway through. Picasso’s twenty-five. He’s painting five women in a brothel. Avignon Street, back in Barcelona. His name for it was The Brothel of Avignon. A writer friend later tidies that up to The Young Ladies of Avignon. Anyway, in the early sketches, there are men in here too. A sailor at a table, and a medical student coming in carrying a skull. Neither man makes it into the painting. So now it’s you the women are facing. His painter friend Georges Braque sees it in the studio. The story goes, he says it’s like being made to drink kerosene. Within a year, Braque paints his own big nude. Before long, the two of them are working out Cubism together. Now look at the woman crouching down on the right. Her back’s turned, but her face comes straight around at you. She didn’t always look like that. Picasso painted over both faces on the right. X-rays show what was there before. A small nose. An ear. Beneath the bridge of the crouching woman’s nose, the X-ray picks up an eye from an earlier face. Years later, Picasso talks about a museum he visited in Paris, right in the middle of working on this. Masks from Africa and the Pacific, brought there through the colonies. He remembers the smell. Says it caught him by the throat. But he stayed. To him, those masks were weapons. Against spirits. He called this his first exorcism.

title: SELF-PORTRAIT WITH TWO FLOWERS IN HER RAISED LEFT HAND
transcript: She’s looking right at you. Kinda like she’s the one sizing you up. That’s Paula Modersohn-Becker. She painted this herself. A year earlier, she’s in Paris, living apart from her husband. Painting herself naked. One of the first modern women artists to do that. In one of those pictures, she gives herself a round belly, as if she’s pregnant. She isn’t. Here, she is. Look at the hand along the bottom. Resting over her belly. And in the other hand, two flowers. A dark red one and a pink one, held right up beside her face. Now get close to that face. The paint’s thick. Ridges across her forehead. Pink around the eyes. That big pink ear. She’s really pushing the stuff around. And there’s another flower. Scratched into her cheek. Probably with the end of her brush. So she’s holding two, and she’s worked another right into her face. She’d been studying Egyptian mummy portraits at the Louvre. Faces painted on wood, placed over the dead. Nearly two thousand years old, some of them. And still, there’s somebody looking out. You can see the connection. The big eyes. The solid, almost masklike face. But hers has all this rough paint sitting on it. You can follow where her hand’s been. She paints this in 1907. That November, she has a daughter. They keep her in bed for eighteen days. That’s what doctors did back then. Then she’s finally allowed up. She combs her hair. Puts in some red roses people brought her. And she walks, slowly, into the living room, where the baby’s in her crib. She picks her up. And suddenly falls to the floor. A blood clot. She’s thirty-one. She made more than seven hundred paintings. Her husband said her last words were “Wie schade.” What a pity.

title: MUSIC (SKETCH)
transcript: Only one of these four people is actually making music. The guy with the violin. The two in the middle are dancing, all wrapped around each other. And the man down on the right is sitting this one out. Head in his hand. Listening. Nobody's looking at anybody. Matisse actually played the violin himself. Years later, his wife asked why he practiced so much. He told her he was afraid of going blind. If he couldn't paint anymore, he could still play. So. Backup plan. Now. This is called Music (Sketch). Look at those black lines. That's charcoal. He's drawing and painting on the same canvas, and he lets you see both. Finished enough to put in a big Paris show, though. He hangs it there in 1907. Gertrude Stein and her brother Leo buy it. Which leaves a question. A sketch for what? Because the big paintings haven't even been ordered yet. That happens two years later. A rich Russian guy wants two enormous paintings for his house in Moscow. One is Music. The other is Dance. In this little one, they're still all together. The violinist. The listener. The dancers. In the big Music, the violinist stays. So does the listener. The dancers... ya know, get their own wall.

title: DANCE (I)
transcript: So, Matisse painted this in less than a week. Nearly thirteen feet across. Five pink naked people dancing on a hill. And he’s still working out the poses while he paints. Get close. The paint’s so thin you can see the weave of the canvas through it. Those faint grey lines beside the arms and legs are places where a body used to be. He changed his mind. Down on the left, where the blue meets the hill, the paint’s run. He leaves that too. Now follow the dancer stretched across the bottom. Her whole body’s reaching for the woman on the left, trying to keep the circle together. Look at the hand she’s reaching for. Barely a hand. More of a smudge. That’s not much of a grip. Blue sky, green hill, five bodies. Hardly a face between them. But you can feel what they’re doing. Nobody had really stripped a painting down this far before. Matisse figured the camera could take care of the details. It was better at them anyway. Painting could get on with the feeling. So where does the dance come from? Not from the famous dancer down the street. He watched her, and his daughter says he found her a bit limited. He pointed to a dance hall in Montmartre instead. Soldiers and workmen going round with their girlfriends. Then a collector from Moscow, Sergei Shchukin, sees this painting. He takes Matisse to lunch, and they work out an order for his staircase. Which makes this enormous thing the sketch. Matisse paints another version. Red bodies this time. That one goes to Russia. This one he keeps. Twenty-seven years. It’s just rolled up in his studio. Like a rug.

title: THE DREAM
transcript: So people had questions about the couch. A naked lady, on a red velvet couch. Ya know, the fancy kind you’d have in a Paris living room. Rousseau’s put it in a jungle. Plants coming up around the arms. Lotus flowers. An elephant peeking out of the leaves. Two lions down below. One’s looking straight at you. And that figure back there, almost lost in the dark. The snake charmer. When Rousseau first shows it, he puts a little poem with it. The woman’s called Yadwigha. She’s fallen asleep, and in her dream she hears the snake charmer’s music. But a critic still wants to know what the furniture’s doing there. So Rousseau writes back. She’s asleep on the couch, dreaming she’s been carried into the forest. That’s why he’s put the couch in. Seems perfectly reasonable to him. Okay, so... we’re inside her dream. Couch and all. Except, look at her eyes. Wide open. Arm stretched out toward the music. Asleep, he says. Anyway, so Rousseau’s been showing at that same exhibition for years, and people laugh. So he asks his poet friend Apollinaire to defend him in print. Avenge him, basically. And Apollinaire does. There’s beauty here, he writes, no arguing with it. Nobody’s going to laugh this year, he says. Ask the painters. Anyway, the jungle’s from the glasshouses in Paris. He said being among those strange plants felt like entering a dream. Then he comes home and paints all this, leaf by leaf. Somebody once counted more than fifty different greens in here. And that name, Yadwigha. The story goes she was a Polish girl he’d loved when he was young. So there may be an old love in this dream, too. He’s an old man by now. She’s young. Stretched out with the lions and the snake, looking pretty comfortable. This is his last big painting. A few months later, he’s dead. And she’s still on that couch. Eyes open. Listening.

title: GIRL WITH A MANDOLIN (FANNY TELLIER)
transcript: Good news. This is the one you can actually see. Start with her head. Tipped down, off to one side, like she's watching her own fingers. Hair up in a bun. Below that, an actual mandolin. The round body, the dark sound hole, the neck climbing up to the right with her fingers on it. In this room, that's practically a photograph. The woman had a name. Fanny Tellier. Posing was her job. She'd sat for some of Picasso's friends, and she offered to sit for him. Then the sittings just kept going. Whatever she signed up for, it wasn't this. So Fanny says she's sick. Then she stops coming altogether. And Picasso stops. You can see that too. Some parts he took all the way. Look at the breast. Round, shaded, downright classical. Other parts get one thin wash of gray and then nothing. The painting quit when she did. And past the name, the record on Fanny is nearly empty. For decades, Picasso didn't even say who she was. Now the strange part. The autumn before, Paris put on a show of Corot. Gentle old landscape painter. Dead before either of them was born. But these were the ones he'd kept back. Figures. Quiet women sitting in studios, holding mandolins more than playing them. Twenty-four of them. Picasso walked through the show with Braque, the guy he was inventing all this with. And within a year, both of them had painted a woman with a mandolin. Braque's is in Madrid. This is Picasso's. The most radical painter in Europe, covering a dead man's tune. Maybe that's what the instrument is doing here. Give somebody a mandolin, and suddenly she can sit there like a pitcher on a table. Years later, somebody called it unfinished. He just shrugged, and said: "I really don't see what I could have added."

title: MAIASTRA
transcript: Alright, so the story goes that Constantin Brancusi walked to Paris from… Bucharest. Fifteen hundred miles. Sleeping outside. Nobody quite agrees how long the whole thing took. Let's call it a year. Supposedly, he arrives on Bastille Day. Later, he writes that France welcomed him with a brass band and a military salute. He's a peasant's kid from the Carpathian Mountains. Three years later, he's working for Rodin. The Thinker guy. Brancusi lasts about a month. "Nothing grows under the shadow of big trees," he says. So he leaves. And a few years later, there's this bird. The Măiastră. A magical bird from Romanian fairy tales. Golden feathers. A song with powers. Exactly what powers… depends on who's telling the story. Here, she's white marble. About two feet tall. Chest out. Neck stretched. Beak aimed at the ceiling. Looks like she's about to let the whole room have it. It's his first bird. He'll make about thirty. But look at what's underneath her. Almost six feet of base. Three times as tall as the bird. Go past that block at the top. Under it. Two people. Rough stone. Barely carved. Holding a rock on their heads. Brancusi made them too. They were a sculpture in their own right. He'd already shown them. Then he puts them to work holding up a bird. It's the first time he builds one sculpture into another. He'll keep doing it for the rest of his life. Now go back up to the bird. Later, he says the hardest part was her head. Getting it up like that without her looking proud. Or like she's picking a fight.

title: THE RED STUDIO
transcript: Imagine Matisse in his studio. Before the red. He's already painted the room once. Blue walls. Pink floor. Yellow furniture. The real walls were white, by the way. He lives with the painting for a while. Then he goes back and does the thing that should wreck it. He covers almost the whole room in red. Not red in the room. Red as the room. Look what he doesn't paint over. His own art. The paintings and sculptures keep their colors while the room around them goes red. But why red? Right after he finished it, a visitor came by and went looking for the red wall. Matisse told him, "This wall does not exist at all!" Where the red came from, he said he didn't know. But he said everything in there only became what it was together with the red. So, let the red hit you first. Then you start finding things. The table. A green plant in a bottle. The chair, barely more than a line. The clock with no hands. And all these paintings inside the painting, still in color. Now, the man in Moscow who'd ordered it never saw the canvas. He asked for a little watercolor of it instead. Matisse sent one, with a letter. The red, he wrote, was a "harmonic link." The man wrote back: "It must be very interesting, but I now prefer your paintings with figures." Matisse kept it for about fifteen years. Then it drifted. Ended up on the wall of a London nightclub, the Gargoyle. Eventually it came to this museum. And when it did, a painter named Mark Rothko started coming here. Just to stand in front of it. For hours. He said when you looked at it, you became the color. You became totally saturated with it.

title: I AND THE VILLAGE
transcript: Alright, here we go. A guy with a bright green face, nose to nose with a cow. And they’re dead serious about it. Locked eyes, a thin line drawn right between them like they’re hashing something out. Then, for no reason, there’s a tiny woman milking a cow, tucked into its cheek. Inside its face. Sure. Up top, a guy with a scythe walks along, and next to him, some lady’s upside down. Arms out. A house sits on its roof. Nobody in here finds any of this the least bit strange. So. Chagall grew up in a Jewish family in Vitebsk. Summers, he’s out at his grandfather’s, in a little town. The kind of place where you basically lived on top of your animals. A cow wasn’t dinner, it was a guy you knew. You fed it, milked it, grew up next to it. So him, going eye to eye with this animal like equals? That’s not a gag. That’s how close it was. Now, everybody wants to call this a dream. A fantasy. He was against all that. What’s inside you, he said, is real. Maybe more real. And memory’s a mess. It doesn’t line up like a photo. It’s everything at once, all the wrong sizes, the important stuff glowing, things floating loose because in your head there’s no up, no down, no clock. He’s not painting the village. He’s painting what it feels like to remember it. By now he’s in Paris, surrounded by Cubists chopping the world into tidy gray cubes. And instead of joining them, he paints this. Green and red and completely impossible. Home, the way it lived inside him. And here’s what the painting couldn’t know yet. Within Chagall’s lifetime, the Holocaust would all but erase this whole world. The crooked little houses. The cow that was a guy you knew. The people. Gone.

title: STILL LIFE WITH AUBERGINES
transcript: Those eggplants have a lot of competition. Look behind them. All that blue and green. Big curls. That’s a screen. Pinned to it on the right, a yellow cloth, different flowers. An orange tablecloth. A pink pot. And that little pale blue man? A plaster anatomy model. Muscles showing. Back then, people thought the original was a Michelangelo. Then, right at the front, three purple eggplants. There they are. The summer Matisse paints this, he’s down south by the sea. He later tells a reporter he walks the hills every day. Keeps trying to paint them. Can’t do it. Too beautiful. Meanwhile, back in the studio, he’s working on a giant version of this. Nearly seven feet tall. A little table. Some eggplants. No hills anywhere. Cloth, though, runs in the family. Generations of weavers. He grows up in a town famous for fancy fabrics. Now, critics have a word for painting like this. And they don’t mean it nicely. Decorative. As in pretty. As in wallpaper. Give it a generation, and American painters are chasing this. But right now, it’s an insult. And Matisse? He says he wants his art to be like a good armchair. That fall, he puts paintings like this into a big Paris show. And the title he gives them? “Decorative sketches.”

title: JEANNETTE (III)
transcript: Start with the one that still looks like somebody you might meet. Then walk along the row. That’s Jeanne. She’s recovering from an illness near the Matisses’ house. While she gets better, she sits for him. In the first one, you’ve got soft cheeks. A face. The second one’s still her. The nose has moved over a bit. You’d probably still recognize her on the street. Now this one. Number three. The first two stop at the neck. Here, he gives her shoulders. A chest. And three big bunches of hair. That one on top looks almost like a beret. Keep going. By the fourth, the face is getting longer. And then there’s the fifth. One eye’s practically a glob. The nose is a blade. And whatever’s happening on top of her head, it’s travelled quite a way from a hairstyle. From the right angle, you’re looking at a bronze maraca. Usually, somebody sits for a bust and expects to recognize themselves. Matisse keeps moving things around. He’s already famous as a painter. Sculpture’s where he works things out. And in clay, if you want to move a cheek, you move it. Five heads. Six years. You can check back with the first one, see how much of Jeanne’s still there. But Jeanne herself only sat for the first two. After that, he’s looking at the heads he’s already made. Now, number five. Years later, when he starts it, he doesn’t work from number four. He goes back to a plaster cast of the third. This one. The shoulders. The three bunches of hair. So it looks like a neat little progression. One, two, three, four, five. He skipped right over four.

title: HOMAGE TO JS BACH
transcript:
There's a name printed on this one.

BACH.

Block capitals, a J and an S underneath. Not painted freehand. Stenciled, the way you'd letter a shipping crate.

The least readable style of painting anybody ever invented, and the one thing you can read is the part he didn't draw. You can see it from across the room.

And the whole painting is smaller than a card table.

Watch what the letters do. Everything around them splinters. Violin scrolls, strings, shards. The letters just sit there. Flat on the surface, refusing to play along.

The cheapest trick here is the one telling the truth.

This whole thing is a flat piece of canvas.

Now look at the left edge. See those ochre stripes, combed like oak?

Braque knew how to do that because Braque painted houses.

His father painted houses. His grandfather painted houses. Georges did the real apprenticeship, ladders and all. Decorator work. Fake wood grain, fake marble. Making cheap walls look expensive.

No brush did that. That's a decorator's graining comb dragged through wet paint. The grooves are still in there.

Far as anyone can tell, this is where fake wood grain enters Cubism.

It got in because Braque owned the comb.

Of course he did. He painted houses.

Why Bach? Braque actually played. Flute, piano. His dealer swore he claimed he could get through Beethoven symphonies on an accordion.

And Bach was his favorite. Past that, he never said.

Then look at the other name. Bottom left, in cursive: G Braque. Something he hardly ever did in these years.

Bach. Braque.

Pretty good. For a house painter.

title: MAN WITH A GUITAR
transcript: Okay, so. Officially, this is a guy playing a guitar. You're gonna have to take Braque's word for that. He's in there somewhere, in that pile of gray and brown. Top left, though, there's a nail. And this fat loop of rope hanging off it. Painted so sharp you want to reach up and unhook it. He's in a hundred pieces, and the realest thing in here is the nail. Not the guy. So. Braque invented Cubism with Picasso. And this is from right at the peak of it. The man's almost gone. Now think about hearing a guitar. You don't get the whole song at once. One note, then the next, and your head glues it together. So, maybe he's painting the guy the way you'd hear him. And that nail's the one thing that doesn't move. Anyway. Now, that rope. Braque and Picasso are in and out of each other's studios every day. Braque said they were like two mountaineers, roped together. Then the war. Braque gets called up. Picasso's Spanish, and Spain sits it out, so he stays. He ends up taking shrapnel to the head. Loses about two years. Even the painting gets drafted. The collector who owns it is German. So France seizes it and later sells it off with a new name. Just Figure. By the time Braque gets back, Picasso's moved on. Braque lives for decades after. And yes, they see each other again. But the way Picasso told it, he took Braque to the station when the war started. And never saw him again.

title: THE ARCHITECT'S TABLE
transcript: This is called The Architect's Table. Except, there's no architect. Honestly, there's barely a table. There's an oval. And inside it, there's a pipe. A bottle. A wine glass. Some sheet music. And a set square. Or, you know, pieces of all those things. Picasso's Cubism has gotten to the point where everything is disappearing into this brown fog of edges and angles. You grab for an object and it kind of slips away. Except, there are two women hiding in here. You don't get their faces. You get their names. The first one, you can't miss. MA JOLIE. Big block letters right across the sheet music. Means "my pretty one." It's from a popular song at the time. But it's also Picasso's nickname for his lover, Eva Gouel. So Eva gets the billboard. And Gertrude? Gertrude gets a calling card. Look down in the lower right. Tiny little painted card. Miss Gertrude Stein. So, one winter day, she stops by Picasso's studio. He's not there. She leaves her card. And Picasso just... paints the thing straight into the picture. Which is such a strange little detail. One woman gets giant letters. The other barely gets a signature. The lover, he shouts. The visitor, he whispers. And then, okay, here's the ending. A couple years later, Gertrude buys the painting. First Picasso she ever bought completely on her own. Her name was already in it.

title: DYNAMISM OF A SOCCER PLAYER
transcript: Okay. Somewhere in here there's a soccer player. Good luck with that one! Six and a half feet of orange and blue going off like a grenade, and a guy who's been more or less deleted by his own speed. These are the Futurists. Italy, around 1913, completely high on the future. Engines, speed, machines, anything loud and new and fast. And they hated the past so much they wanted the museums burned down. Called them cemeteries. Boccioni was their big painter, and the whole point was to kill the one thing painting always did. Hold a body still so you can look at it. He wanted the opposite. Make it move. Make it come apart. They had other plans too. Figured a good war would scrub the world clean and start it fresh. So when the real one showed up, they signed up thrilled. Here's how that goes for the painter of pure speed. He's thirty-three, in training, and he falls off a horse. Not the war. A horse. The fastest mind in Italy, taken out by the slowest thing in the army. And yeah, some of this future-worship runs straight into Fascism later. So no, you don't get to call it innocent. But the painting still works. That's the uncomfortable part. The player's still in there. Still moving. The one thing in the whole building that won't hold still. Which is exactly what they wanted. They just didn't picture the wall. White paint, a guard a few feet off, a little label with his name. One of the cemeteries they swore they'd burn. Permanent collection now.

title: THE BLUE WINDOW
transcript: Everything’s blue. The walls. The table. The trees outside. Even the sky, which at least has an excuse. Now, you’re in the bedroom. The garden’s out there. Usually, the window helps keep track of that. Try finding it. There are clues. But the tabletop and the sky are practically the same blue. And see that yellow head sitting on the table? Follow the black line coming out of it. Straight up. Is that the window frame? Or a tree trunk? It’s doing both jobs. Then there’s the green lamp. With what looks like a tree growing out of it. Somebody once asked Matisse on the radio why he painted so many windows. He said he didn’t separate inside from outside. From the horizon right into the room, it was all one space. And this is his room. The bedroom he shares with his wife, Amélie. Her dressing table. Her flowers. Down in the corner, her little brooch in a dish. All soaked in blue. Now look outside. That pale building with a touch of yellow. His studio. The only painting where he shows it from the outside. So you’re standing where he sleeps, looking toward where he works. Same blue all the way through. Matisse said he originally meant this for a Paris fashion designer. The designer says no. Too advanced for him. The next spring, the painting appears in a magazine. With a different title. La Glace sans tain. A mirror without its silver backing. The stuff that makes it reflect. Take that off, and you can see through it. A window.

title: AGAPANTHUS
transcript: Look at those stems. Long, bending arcs. Little purple flowers at the ends. And all that green, with blue coming through it. Agapanthus. Monet planted them along his pond at Giverny. In his thirties, he was out making those quick, bright landscapes that helped get Impressionism going. Now he's in his seventies. He's got the garden. Six full-time gardeners. But his wife has died. He's barely painting. Then he gets going again. Huge canvases. The pond. Everything growing along the banks. This one's taller than you are. And his eyes are going. Cataracts. He tells an interviewer he's choosing his paints by the labels on the tubes. Monet. Having to check which one's blue. Now look how much blue he's put in here. One of his closest friends is Georges Clemenceau. France's prime minister at the end of the First World War. The day after the Armistice, Monet writes to him. He wants to give France two big paintings. His only way, he says, of taking part in the victory. Two paintings becomes twenty-two. They end up in two oval rooms in Paris. This one stays at Giverny. His son keeps it. Now, Clemenceau also trained as a doctor. And Monet's been told he needs surgery on those eyes. He's afraid it'll blind him. So he keeps putting it off. Then Clemenceau writes him a letter. Says Monet taught him to understand light. "My eyes need your color." When Monet dies, they put a black cloth over the coffin. Clemenceau sees it. "No black for Monet." He finds an old cloth in the house to use instead. The colors of forget-me-nots. Periwinkles. Hydrangeas.

title: WATER LILIES
transcript: One of Monet’s gardeners worked from a boat. Dust kept blowing in off the road and settling on the water, and Monet wanted clean reflections. So somebody had to literally dust the pond. He’d had it dug in the first place so he’d have something to paint. And here’s nearly forty-two feet of it, with no bank, no horizon. The only sky is the one in the water. Try those pale patches in the middle. They’re clouds. Follow one for a moment, and you’re looking down into something deep. Then you notice a leaf, and you’re back on the surface. Same stretch of paint, doing both. Get closer, and even the water disappears. You’ve just got thick paint, scrubbed paint, one color dragged through another. He builds a whole studio for these during the First World War. He writes a friend that some days he feels ashamed, painting his pond while all those people are dying. He keeps going until he dies. Then, for years, the paintings just sit in the studio. People think they’re too messy. During the next war, Giverny gets bombarded. Glass and metal fall onto the canvases and cut into them. Somebody patches the cuts with tape. Then, in the fifties, painters in New York are working huge. Pollock, with paint going right out to the edges. Suddenly, messy looks right. This museum, which had mostly left Monet out of its story of modern art, finally wants one. A curator, Dorothy Miller, and a colleague go pick one out at Monet’s studio. Alfred Barr wires back, in telegram-speak: BUY MONET IF YOU DOROTHY REALLY LIKE. They do. The museum buys it. Three years later, the building catches fire. A worker dies. The Monet’s too big to move, and it’s destroyed. Afterward, Dorothy goes looking for another. She finds this one in another painter’s studio in Paris, tape still on the cuts. Back in New York, conservators vacuum thirty years of dust off the back. Then they put the cut threads back together, thread to thread. Nearly forty-two feet of pond. Go on. See if you can find a repair.

title: GARE MONTPARNASSE (THE MELANCHOLY OF DEPARTURE)
transcript: Okay. We got a train station. A clock up on a brick tower. Stuck at twenty-seven past one. An empty square. A little train on the horizon, puffing smoke. Two tiny figures way off, just standing there. And down in the corner, a pile of bananas. Green ones. Not even ripe. Just sitting there like they know something. For about one second, it all looks normal. Then it tips. Look at the ground on the right, ramping up too steep, too fast. The arcade on the left pulls one way, the building behind it pulls another. The wind's whipping the flags on that tower. But the train's smoke goes straight up. Nothing lines up. That's the trick. The bananas are a decoy. The thing crawling up your back is the geometry. He built a place that can't exist, and painted it like it's the most normal thing in the world. And he called it The Melancholy of Departure. Like, you can't even tell if that train's coming or going, but you already miss it. He painted it in early 1914. Here's the kicker. De Chirico is twenty-five. Twenty-five, and he's already found a frequency nobody else can hear yet. Empty plazas. Long shadows. Ya know that feeling when nobody's following you, but you pick up the pace anyway. A few years later, the Surrealists find this. Dalí, Magritte, Ernst, all of them walk through this exact door. And by the time they move in, he's gone. He drops the whole thing, goes classical, starts painting like it's three hundred years ago. They turn on him. But, the painting already did its job. It built the room. They moved in later. He'd already moved out. A few years later, he finds out these early paintings are still the ones people want. So he makes more. Sometimes he gives the new ones old dates. This one really is from 1914. Some of the later ones? Same artist. But wrong year. There's an Italian word for them. Verifalsi. True fakes.

title: TABLEAU NO. 2 / COMPOSITION NO. V
transcript: Alright, try following one of those black lines all the way across, through all that pink and dusty yellow. Good luck. Now look a little up and left of center. That tiny cross. And above the middle, there's a shape with a rounded top. Kinda like an arch. This might have started with a church. Notre-Dame-des-Champs. Near Mondrian's studio in Paris. But there's not much church left. Picasso's in the same neighborhood, taking guitars apart. And Mondrian's seeing how much of the thing you can lose. Eventually, he gets to those grids he's famous for. Even his name gets shorter. Look at the signature, bottom left. Back home, it was Mondriaan. Two a's. Paris just gets one. And look at the corners. Everything's crowded into the middle, and out toward the edges, the lines start giving out. Just gray. It's 1914. That summer, he goes home to Holland for a couple of weeks. Meanwhile, a gallery in The Hague's got a whole show of his new Paris paintings up. He gets there for the last week. A Rotterdam paper notices the new spelling. Then says the paintings look like the floor plan of a pig market. He's hoping to sell one. Enough for the rent. A preacher from Gouda buys three. This is one of them. Then, the week the show closes, the First World War starts. Mondrian wants to go back. But that means the long way round, through England or Germany. Which is expensive. And everybody figures it'll be over soon. So he stays. His studio's in Paris. His paints too. In Holland, he starts making drawings of the North Sea. With the pier sticking out into it. And he's doing to that view what he was doing to buildings back in Paris. Breaking it down. Same short, stop-and-start marks. Horizontals for the water. Verticals for the pier. He's gone from a church to the sea. And he keeps finding these lines. Meanwhile, he's still paying rent on that Paris studio. He was just coming home for a couple of weeks. The visit lasts five years.

title: GUITAR
transcript: Okay, find the hole in the middle of this guitar. On a real guitar, that’s nothing, ’cause, ya know… it’s a hole. Here, it’s a little tube. Sticking straight out at you. Hang on to that. Now look at what the whole thing’s made of. A few pieces of sheet metal, cut and bent. Some wires for strings. Back then, sculpture meant carving it out of stone, or modeling it in clay and casting it. Either way, you start with a solid lump of something and find the thing inside. Picasso’s a painter. The one who’d already broken painting into pieces. He looks at all that and goes, nah. He doesn’t carve it. Doesn’t mold it. He builds it. Like a kid with a cereal box. First out of cardboard, paper and string, and he hangs it on his studio wall, right in with his drawings. Then he does it all again in sheet metal. This one. A poet says people who came by the studio asked: Does it go on a pedestal, or on the wall? Is it a painting, or a sculpture? And Picasso, the story goes, just says: “It’s nothing. It’s a guitar.” Then he keeps it for almost sixty years before he gives it to MoMA. Now look at the wall behind it. The shadows. Painters fake those for a living. This one makes its own. So go back to that hole. Picasso said that tube came from an African mask. A Grebo mask, with eyes that poke out at you.

title: PAINTERLY REALISM OF A BOY WITH A KNAPSACK
transcript: Okay so. The title of this thing is longer than the actual painting. You ready? "Painterly Realism of a Boy with a Knapsack. Color Masses in the Fourth Dimension." And the painting? A black square. And a little red one. That's it. That's the whole thing. So, uh, where's the boy. Where's the knapsack. Yeah, there's no boy. Never was gonna be one. He sticks this giant cosmic name on two little squares on purpose, and that gap, between the huge title and the two shapes, that's the bit. Except he's not kidding. He means every word. This is 1915. He's just cooked up a thing he calls Suprematism. His own description: he'd boiled himself down to "the zero of form" and "escaped from the circle of things." Which, translated out of guru, means a painting doesn't have to be a picture of anything anymore. No boy, no apple, no saint. Just shapes. Just color. Hanging there. And get this. He called it realism. Straight up. "New painterly realism," his phrase. Like, two squares are more real than a painting of a boy, not less. And, honestly? Kind of has a point. The squares aren't faking anything. They're not pretending to be a guy, or a window, or a nice day in the country. A square's just a square. Can't lie to you. So look at 'em. Big black square. Little red one. Tipped a bit, floating on all that white. He's not painting a thing. He's painting a thing with nothing in it. And here's the real move. The show where these first go up, 1915, he sticks a plain black square way up high in the corner of the room. Now, in a Russian house, that corner's got exactly one job. It's where the religious icon goes. The holy picture. So everybody who walks in just gets it. He's not hanging a painting. He's hanging a religion. A black square, right where God used to be. So, yeah. Either it's the most pretentious thing a person's ever done with a ruler and two colors. Or it's one of the gutsiest. With this guy, it's both. He looked at everything painting had ever done, all the kings and saints and bowls of fruit, and just went, nah. Start over. From a black square. And a name three sizes too big.

title: THE PIANO LESSON
transcript: This one, you need the year. 1916. France is deep in the war. Matisse has tried to enlist. Bought the boots and everything. They turn him down. Twice. Too old. Weak heart. His mother’s alone in the occupied north. His brother’s in a prison camp. He’s sold prints to send them bread. A hundred kilos a week. And his two boys are getting close to military age. Here’s one of them. Pierre. Sixteen. At home, practicing the piano. The painting’s eight feet tall. And not one thing in it about the war. Find his head, over on the right. Just above the music. One eye looking out at you. The other disappears under that gray triangle. So, who’s giving the lesson? That person sitting up there, all upright with no face. Looks like somebody’s keeping an eye on him. But that’s another painting. Hanging on the living room wall. Matisse has flattened the room. Cut it into hard edges and angles. He’s borrowing from Cubism. Picasso’s territory. Picasso said nobody looked at his paintings as closely as Matisse. And nobody looked at Matisse’s as closely as Picasso. And here he is, using it on his own son. Now find the metronome. On the piano. There’s your teacher. Another triangle. Like the one cutting into Pierre’s face. And with everything else so still, you can almost hear it. Tick. Tick. Tick. The next summer, Matisse’s older boy signs up. He’s going to work on airplanes. Matisse writes to a painter friend. “Something important has happened in my house.” “Jean, my eldest, has left to join the regiment at Dijon.”

title: FROM THE VIADUCT, 125TH STREET, NEW YORK
transcript: Okay. 1916. A twenty-five-year-old kid hauls a camera the size of a suitcase up onto a viaduct over 125th Street. And instead of pointing it out at the city, like a normal person, he aims it straight down. At the sidewalk. He didn't make any of this. He found it. The shadow was really there. The light actually did that. Two men really were standing on that corner, mid-conversation. A painter could invent a scene like this. Strand had to catch one. And he's got maybe a couple minutes before the sun moves and it's gone. Look what he goes for. Not the street. Not the two guys. The shadow. That big dark web of girders crossing the pavement. He aimed a machine built to record the truth at a sidewalk, and came back with pure geometry. He didn't photograph a place. He photographed a shape. And in 1916, that's not what photographs do. A photo's supposed to be a picture of something. A person, a view, a moment you keep. Strand hands you an abstraction. Stieglitz, the most powerful man in American photography, takes one look and gives this kid the entire last issue of his magazine, Camera Work. Like: everybody, look. This is where it's going. And here's the wild part. It's all real. Soft and hazy as it is, every line in it actually happened. For a few minutes, on a corner nobody'd look at twice, the city folded into a diagram. And this kid was up there, looking down, ready. Click. Gone. Except he kept it.

title: THE MOROCCANS
transcript: Kind of a strange one… coming from the color guy. Look at all that black. A big empty field of it, right through the middle. Matisse spent two winters in Tangier, in Morocco. He was always going south for the light. And down there, it’s brutal. Then, back in France, he paints what he remembers. Up on the left, a white dome behind a balcony. Over on the right, all that dusty pink, and a man in a white turban, with his back to us. Now, those green lumps down below. They kinda look like melons? Or are they bowed backs and heads of guys praying? Matisse said melons. Watermelons and gourds. Other people see men praying. You can flip between them all day. He carried the idea around for years. Sketched it in a letter home to his wife, from Tangier. By the time he finishes it, he’s in a studio outside Paris. And out east, at a place called Verdun, France and Germany are in the longest battle of the First World War. They’re dying by the thousands. And there’s all that black. Easy to read it as gloom. But that’s not how Matisse explained it. Thirty-odd years later, he said this was where his blacks began. Black didn’t have to mean shadow. Or night. He said the big black in his Moroccans glowed as much as any color in it. He’d painted light with it. Even the light of Tangier.

title: FOUNTAIN
transcript: So, this is the urinal they wouldn't let into a show that was supposed to let everybody in. New York. Thousands of artworks. No jury. No prizes. Pay the fee, you're in. That was the deal. Now the directors are in a meeting, trying to work out what to do about a urinal. Somebody's signed it R. Mutt. Some say it's indecent. Others say, well, we did say everybody. They take a vote. Out. One of the directors resigns. Marcel Duchamp. Keep that name in mind. Now look at the thing. A store-bought urinal. Turned on its back. Little holes where the water comes through. And there on the rim, in black paint: R. Mutt. A fake name. The usual story is, Duchamp sent it in himself. Duchamp and some friends put out a magazine. The editorial takes up Mr. Mutt's case. Whether he made it himself "has no importance." "He chose it." Duchamp calls these readymades. He said he went for the thing with the least chance of being liked. Years later, there's another vote. Five hundred art experts. Most influential modern artwork. The urinal wins. Picasso comes second. But there's something else about Mr. Mutt. The day after the show opens, Duchamp writes to his sister. Says a female friend sent it in under a man's name. Doesn't say which friend. Some people think he means Baroness Elsa, another Dada artist. That argument's still going. And the original? Disappeared. The ones in museums are copies Duchamp approved decades later. The best look we've got at the first one is a photograph. Alfred Stieglitz took it. Put it on a pedestal in his gallery. In front of a painting. Made a picture. Two weeks after they throw it out, Stieglitz writes to a friend. Everybody who's seen the photograph, he says, thinks it's beautiful. "A cross between a Buddha and a veiled woman."

title: COMPOSITION WITH COLOR PLANES 5
transcript: Pink. That's the first problem. You think you know Mondrian. Red. Yellow. Blue. Thick black lines. This one has pink. No black. Not even a proper grid. It's 1917. The Mondrian in your head hasn't been invented yet. He's living in Laren, a village in Holland. Nearby is another painter named Bart van der Leck. Van der Leck had worked in stained glass. So he already knew what color looked like when it didn't have to pretend to be skin or sky or a vase. Red could just be red. Yellow could just be yellow. Mondrian's own paintings were doing something else. The trees and oceans were disappearing. You had to work harder and harder to find what the painting had started as. Each man sees the part he doesn't have. So they start stealing from each other. Mondrian takes the color. Van der Leck takes the nerve to let the subject disappear. Fair trade. And for a minute, they meet right here. Composition with Color Planes 5. One big mustard-yellow block in the middle. Pink and gray around it. The white isn't background. It cuts in between the colors. And nobody has built the black fence yet. That same year, they help start a magazine. De Stijl. "The Style." Not "A Style." "The." That is a lot of confidence for a group still deciding whether pink stays. The next year, there's a manifesto to sign. Mondrian signs it. Van der Leck doesn't. He helped invent "The Style." He just didn't agree with the rules. Van der Leck eventually lets recognizable things back in. Trees. Flowers. A man on a horse. Mondrian goes the other way. He keeps getting stricter. The black grid arrives. The pink goes.

title: WHITE ON WHITE
transcript: “Swim in the white free abyss, infinity is before you.” That’s Kazimir Malevich. This is one of his white paintings. A white square on a white square. Which sounds like nothing. So, look closer. The background’s warm, almost cream. The square’s cool, almost gray. Tipped a little. A few years before, he paints a black square on white. He calls it Suprematism. Basically, a painting doesn’t have to show anything anymore. Shapes and colors alone can make you feel something. Then he goes further. Even the black goes. Okay, so, quick history lesson. After the Russian Revolution, the new government hands guys like Malevich their own art schools. Ten years later, Stalin’s taking over. And they want paintings everybody can, ya know… understand. So… Malevich takes about seventy works to a show in Berlin. A month in, he gets called back home. And he figures he’s in trouble. He even writes a will, in case he ends up dead, or in prison. And he leaves the paintings with an architect friend. He never sees them again. Three years later, the man who painted nothing gets arrested. Questioned about that trip. Let go. And this one? The architect passes them to a museum man. When the Nazis come in, he puts them in storage. So this “free abyss” is now sitting in the dark. Then this guy Alfred Barr, from the brand-new Museum of Modern Art, comes through and buys two. This one included. He sneaks them over the border. In a suitcase, and a couple of canvases rolled up inside his umbrella. Was this one in the umbrella? Nobody knows. But the painting gets out. That same year, Malevich dies. His friends drive his coffin down the main street on an open truck. And on the front of the truck… a black square.

title: ENDLESS COLUMN, VERSION I
transcript: One shape. Fat in the middle, pinched at both ends. Like a big wooden bead. Stack it. Then stack it again. That’s Brancusi’s Endless Column. And the whole thing is carved oak. You can still see the chisel marks. Now look at the top. The last shape gets cut off halfway through. Same at the bottom. It doesn’t end. It just... stops. And your eye keeps adding pieces, right up through the ceiling. Ya know, usually, a sculpture stands on a pedestal. Brancusi had been using shapes like these underneath his sculptures. Then he starts making the base the whole thing. Nothing on top. Just more base. He makes more columns over the years. Taller ones. The same shape, over and over. Then, in the thirties, a group of women back home in Romania asks the local boy who made it big in Paris to make a war memorial. The Women’s League of Gorj. His home county. So, during the First World War, German troops had tried to cross the bridge at Targu Jiu. Local people helped defend it. Old men, women, kids. Held them off until reinforcements arrived. Now they want something to remember the people who died defending the town. And Brancusi gives them this shape. Cast in iron. Almost a hundred feet tall. Out in the open, with the sky above it. And right at the top, the same half-shape. Already widening out again. Anyway, come back to this one. Six foot eight. It’s the earliest one anybody still has.

title: THE CITY
transcript: Okay. Quick Léger fact. He spent three years of the war digging trenches in the Argonne. Shells going over his head the whole time. And the thing he wrote about wasn't the fear. It was the breech of a 75 millimeter cannon with the sun on it. "The magic of light on the white metal." His words. The deadliest object in France, and he's standing there thinking, that is gorgeous. Then he gets gassed, spends a year in a hospital, and comes home. And this is what he paints about it. The City. 1919. No trenches anywhere. Billboards. Scaffolding. A staircase. A giant letter B with no word attached. Full volume. Now find the people. Two of them, down by the stairs, dead center. Flat. Dark. No faces. Then look at the posters. The blue guy in the billboard on the right has more color than the actual humans. Maybe that's a complaint. Doesn't feel like one. Feels like a man who walked out of the war still in love with the machine that almost killed him. He just stopped pretending people stood outside it. There's no horizon in here, by the way. No place to stand, no view. There's even a big purple pole planted right in the middle, blocking the best part. Cities do that. You don't look at this city. It hits you. Which is the honest version. Nobody sees a city. You're just in one, and it's loud, and somewhere a sign is shouting half a word at you. He thought all that was worth loving. Stand here a minute. Hard not to.

title: SPATIAL CONSTRUCTION NO. 12
transcript: Alright, Rodchenko. The great quitter of modern art. The guy doesn't drift away from stuff, he just ends it. A year or so after this, he puts up three canvases in Moscow. One's just red. One's just yellow. One's just blue. And he announces, that's it, it's all over. Painting, taken to its logical conclusion. His words. Then he actually quits. Walks off, makes ads, takes pictures. This is also a man who designed his own work jumpsuit, pockets everywhere for the tools, had his wife sew it, and wore it to teach his classes. Because that was the whole idea after the Revolution. No more genius in a smock. An artist is an engineer now. They even called themselves Constructivists. Builders. So look what the engineer built. One flat sheet of plywood. That's it, that's the material. Ovals drawn inside ovals, cut out, fanned into space, tied with wire. The whole recipe fits on an index card. Which was the point. He doesn't even give it a title, he gives it a number. Spatial Construction number 12. Like a part in a catalog. And it hangs from the ceiling, because pedestals were for the old guys. Get up close, look at the inner rings. Still kind of silver, right? Aluminum paint. It was supposed to catch the light while it turned, he called the series Light-Reflecting Surfaces. The outer rings are back to plain wood. That part's just time. Now, 1921. A room in Moscow, hung full of these things. The big show, the one that launched them. Everything we know about that room comes from two photographs. Two. Almost nothing in those pictures still exists. One little piece by another guy. And this. Funny thing, though. You could build one of these tonight. Same sheet, same cuts, same wire. And it wouldn't count. Everyone knows it wouldn't. Only the original counts. Which is the exact feeling Rodchenko spent his life trying to kill. It grew back anyway. On this one. Not bad for an index card.

title: THE NEWBORN, VERSION I
transcript: Alright, so get down to its level. It’s about eight inches long. Like something from a spaceship. Or a... droid egg thing. It’s from 1920, and it looks like it hasn’t even been invented yet. And be honest. You’d like to put it in your pocket. Now look at the front. Like somebody’s sliced the end off an egg. Except there’s a little curl left at the bottom. That’s a chin. And that big flat bit? A mouth. Wide open. It’s a baby. If you’ve ever held one while it’s screaming, you know the shape. The whole head goes mouth. Constantin Brancusi made it. Romanian, living in Paris. One of the guys who basically invented modern sculpture. He’s been making children’s heads for years. The early ones look like actual children. You’d know what you were looking at from across the room. Then the heads get simpler. The neck goes. The hair. The ears. More and more of the face. By 1915, he’s carved one in marble that’s down to this. An egg with a cry coming out of it. He calls it The Newborn. Five years later, this bronze. Polished like a mirror. You can still practically hear it. Anyway, he gives this one away. A wedding present to a young couple in Paris. They take it home to New York. A screaming baby. For the newlyweds. MoMA buys it from the bride. Now come back to that shiny surface. Get a little closer. There’s your face. Right in the scream.

title: THREE MUSICIANS
transcript: Look at these guys. Three of them, crammed together, mid-song. Big. Loud. Having a blast. And then you find out who they might be. And it stops being quite so fun. The harlequin in the middle, the one in the diamonds, that's Picasso. On the guitar. He painted himself as the harlequin over and over, so that one's pretty hard to miss. The other two, nobody can prove it, but they've usually been read as his two close friends. The poet Apollinaire, in the white Pierrot getup, on the clarinet. And the other poet, Max Jacob, dressed as a monk, with the sheet music. By the time Picasso paints this, Apollinaire's dead. Died young, two days before the war ended. Max Jacob's still around. But that same year, he'd left Paris and gone off to live near a monastery. Basically, like a monk. So Picasso's got one friend who's dead. One friend who's gone. And what does he do? He paints them back. Sticks all three of them in one room, hands out the instruments, starts the band up again. Like nothing happened. And the thing is so bright, so happy, you almost miss how sad it is. Grief showing up in a clown suit. Then look at the bodies. Try to find where one guy ends and the next one starts. You can't. Picasso runs into Apollinaire. Apollinaire runs into Jacob. All of them run into the walls. Maybe that's the whole trick. He's got these three friends back together, and he's not giving anybody enough room to leave. And there's a fourth one in this band. A big dog. Head far left. Body under the table. Tail by the harlequin's legs. Everything else in here is shouting. And the dog just stays low and quiet.

title: THREE WOMEN
transcript: Okay, so look at that black animal behind the woman on the right. The wall label says cat. MoMA's own book says dog. And there's a letter from the painter about this picture. So, he might have some idea. Léger writes to Alfred Barr at MoMA about this painting. He'd painted The City. Buildings, signs, everything jammed together. Then he wanted the opposite. "A contrary force," he said. So he made, in his words, "an easel painting." Six feet by eight. That's one serious easel. Anyway, so he takes an old favorite. Three naked women on a couch. One's got a book open on her lap and a spoon in her cup. Nothing much happening. But look at her arms. Big, smooth tubes. Then that black rail across the sofa. Another tube. The other two, even their hair looks like polished metal. "The classical won," he tells Barr. So the women are there the way the cups and the furniture are. A human body, he said, counts for about as much as a set of keys. Now, about that animal. He's writing in English. The English gets a little tangled. Says he wanted subjects "treated during all the times by painters of other times." Then he gives Barr a little list. "Some women's bodies, one table, a dog."

title: COMPOSITION WITH RED, BLUE, BLACK, YELLOW, AND GRAY
transcript: Mondrian thought paintings like this could help fix society. But...Paris wasn't buying it. Ya know, Actually buying it. It's 1921. His abstract paintings are a tough sell. So he paints flowers, too. Petals. Stems. A rose that looks like a rose. They help pay the bills. Then he goes back to this. Red. Blue. Black. Yellow. Gray. Put "Composition with" in front of that and you've got the title. Like a paint-store receipt. Look at that black block down at the bottom. The huge stretch of gray up on the right. Then the yellow. One little square, squeezed into the corner. Hardly any yellow at all. But your eye still goes there. Nothing matches. Somehow, it holds together. And Mondrian thinks that balance could work outside a painting. In buildings. Furniture. The way people live together. Which is a lot to put on a yellow square. But three years later, Gerrit Rietveld builds the Schröder House in the Netherlands. White walls. Black lines. Red, blue, yellow. It looks like a Mondrian you can walk into. Try that with a rose.
