When Peter dies, David asks everyone else to leave the room. He has a camera with him. He photographs Peter's face. His hands. His feet. Peter took this one. David took those. At the funeral, Fran Lebowitz said Peter had hung up on every important photography dealer in the Western world. He said once, "When people talk about me, I want them to be whispering." Outside downtown, while he was alive, his pictures mostly went unnoticed. The younger artists noticed. Nan Goldin. And this guy. Everybody else took a while. David turned into one of the loudest artists of the AIDS years. Five years after Peter, he died of AIDS too. And this photograph? David gave it to the museum.

title: GOVERNMENT APPROVED HOME FALLOUT SHELTER SNACK BAR
transcript: Okay so, in 1980, the federal government put out instructions for turning your basement rec-room into a fallout shelter. There's a snack bar in it. Actual FEMA pamphlet. So in '83, Michael Smith built the thing. Smith and a set designer named Alan Herman. They put it in a gallery in New York. Wood paneling. Linoleum. Easy chair. Records. Barrels of survival crackers. Liquor bottles. Basically, the basement at the end of the world. And the bar has a canopy on hinges. Fold it down, pile concrete blocks on top, and now it's a radiation shield. That part's straight out of the pamphlet. Smith even had a word for the menu. Cuisine. Because nuclear war, he said, is this great democratizing event. Rich guy, poor guy, everybody ends up in the same basement eating the same crackers. So, Smith had been playing this character named Mike since the late seventies. Mike started out as Blandman. A guy basically built to be bland. Mike follows instructions. Mike believes the brochure. And this time, the brochure was real. Oh, and there's one more thing down there. An arcade game. Working joystick. Coin slot. It's called Mike Builds a Shelter. Smith made it with a graphics designer and a teenager who coded the whole thing on a Commodore 64. You play Mike. You put your coin in and the air-raid sirens start. Little 8-bit Mike, carrying three concrete blocks down the stairs before the big one drops. And the game is programmed so nobody can win. Every game ends the same way. Manhattan gets nuked. Then the theme from Dr. Strangelove starts playing.

title: TEARS
transcript: America's getting ready to throw itself a five-hundred-year party. The Columbus quincentennial. Five hundred years since a European guy showed up. Kay WalkingStick is Cherokee. She said she couldn't possibly celebrate Columbus. So she makes this. Small enough to carry in your arms. Four black poles. A platform. A little bundle lying on top. And some words on the base. It's a model of a funerary scaffold. WalkingStick described how Native people who moved with the seasons would lay their dead on a platform like this and burn them. The ashes return to nature. The smoke rises. Something going down. Something going up. Now look at that bundle. It's meant to look like a person. Inside, there's a corn husk. Some turquoise. A few stones. And the leather around it came from a shirt. One she'd made for her husband, Michael. They'd been married thirty years. He died suddenly, the year before she made this. She still had the shirt. So that's what she wraps around the little figure. Then underneath the platform, where the fire would go, she puts a copper plate. It says: "In 1492, we were twenty million. Now, we are two million." And then a question. "Where are the generations?"

title: DEODORIZED CENTRAL MASS WITH SATELLITES
transcript: You get the smell first. Pine. The industrial kind. The kind that means somebody has cleaned something. Then you look up, and for a second it's actually kind of beautiful. Big fuzzy balls hanging from the ceiling on wires you can hardly see. Blue. Green. Yellow. Planets. That's where your brain goes. Somebody put a solar system in a white room. And these shiny pointed things down both walls. Like pieces off a very expensive car. Kelley called it Deodorized Central Mass with Satellites. The satellites are obvious. The deodorized part is waiting on the walls. Get closer. Stuffed animals. Hundreds of them, sewn into balls. Sorted by color, like laundry. And every one is facing inward. No eyes. No little noses. Nothing in there to make eye contact with. Kelley did that on purpose. He didn't want them pulling sentiment out of you. He'd been working with stuffed animals since 1987. Thrift stores, yard sales. The places objects go after they've been demoted from loved to tolerated to disposable. He thought he was making work about commodity culture. The things we buy to stand in for love. Nobody heard that. They saw the matted fur and the stains and went straight to childhood trauma. Somebody slept with this thing. Cried into it. Carried it through the worst years of being small. Then one day, gone. And they looked at the man sewing them together and decided something terrible must have happened to him. Kelley said he was stunned. Then he did the strangest possible thing. He went with it. If everybody believed buried abuse was hiding underneath the work, fine. He took their diagnosis and started working with that. Repressed memories. Buried trauma. America digging through the child to explain the adult. This one stretches from 1991 to 1999, right through the middle of all that. Now look at the ten shiny shapes on the walls. Kelley called them deodorizers. Every few minutes, pssshhht. Pine. The animals bring in everything messy. Dirt. Memory. Shame. Love. The tasteful modern objects keep trying to clean it up. Forever. Read MoMA's list of materials. Plush toys. Wood. Wire. Styrofoam. Rope. Pulleys. Car paint. And disinfectant.

title: PARADOX OF PRAXIS 1 (SOMETIMES MAKING SOMETHING LEADS TO NOTHING)
transcript: Alright, here's the plan, in full. Get a block of ice. A big one. Mexico City. 1997. Now push it through the streets. No cart. No rope. Start with your hands. Keep going until there's nothing left to push. Francis Alÿs did this for more than nine hours. Nine hours. That's not a gesture. That's a shift. Somewhere in the middle it stops being impressive and starts being a question. He announced the answer in advance. It's the title. Paradox of Praxis 1: Sometimes Making Something Leads to Nothing. At first, the ice is heavy. It fights him. People have to step around this man shoving a perfect white block through traffic. Then, hour by hour, the job gets easier. Exactly as fast as the point of it disappears. Soon he can push it with one hand. Then kick it with his foot. Near the end, the block is the size of an ice cube. Then it's a wet spot. Then Mexico City just keeps being Mexico City. Alÿs had moved there about a decade earlier. An architect who stopped building things. A lot of his work runs on this. Enormous effort, tiny result. Which, depending on the week you're having, is either absurd or extremely familiar. He wasn't mocking it. He was rehearsing it. On purpose. In public. Nine hours of pushing. The video runs five minutes.

title: ŁÓDŹ, OCTOBER 1, 2004
transcript: So, Christopher Williams doesn't take his own pictures. He hires a commercial photographer. Somebody who shoots catalogs. Williams sets it all up. Somebody else presses the button. And MoMA still gave him a whole retrospective. His dad worked in special effects in Hollywood. So he grew up on film sets, watching people manufacture things you were supposed to believe. He wanted to get away from all that. Got himself a painting studio. Sat there alone. Missed the set. So, back came the photographers. The lights. The whole production. Only now he's running it. He's not really after the pretty picture. He's after the stuff that makes them. And the pictures look like ads. Almost. A mole on a model's face. Laugh lines. Little things an ad might clean up. He leaves them. Now look at the cloth here. White, with little blue squares. Coming off the rollers, folding into a stack on a cart. Spotless. You could put it straight in a catalog. Then look at the room it's coming out of. Plaster peeling off. Brick showing through. A bare tube light. Plastic draped over the machine. A catalog photographer would find a way to lose all that. Williams wants it in the picture. The place is falling apart. And that cloth has no idea. This is Łódź, in Poland. For over a century, this was the country's cloth town. And Williams calls the whole series For Example. The rest of the title comes from a French book about two ways of running an industrial country. Capitalism, or Soviet planning. This town's tried both. Private owners ran the mills. After the war, the state took over. Then the Soviet bloc came apart. And the cloth business went with it. But look at that stack. On October first, two thousand four, somebody here was still making it.

title: WALL DRAWING #1144, BROKEN BANDS OF COLOR IN FOUR DIRECTIONS
transcript: A man walks into a brand-new gallery carrying a pencil. That's it. No canvas. No crate coming in behind him. He walks up to a bare white wall and starts drawing directly on the building. October 1968. Prince Street, before SoHo was really SoHo. The gallery's first show. The whole thing is a benefit. The money goes to a committee trying to end the war in Vietnam. And on the price list, every other artwork has a number. Sol LeWitt's says: by the hour. Which is, uh, a pretty strange way to sell a drawing. You're paying a man with a pencil to make an idea show up. That first drawing is gone. And, okay, this one can go the same way. Thirty-seven feet of color. Broken bands heading off in four directions. Bright. Orderly. Almost stupidly cheerful. LeWitt didn't draw it. He wrote down the decisions. Colors. Directions. What goes where. Then other people climbed the ladders and made it happen. Instructions go in. Something like stained glass comes out. And when the museum is finished with it, they can just paint the whole thing white. No storage crate. Just a roller. Gone. And, somehow, MoMA still owns the artwork. Because the wall is only where the work is visiting. The plan survives. Take it to another wall and, you know, the whole thing comes back. Different wall. Different hands. Same work. That was the trick. LeWitt kept removing things people thought an artist had to do. Touch the work. Be in the room. Eventually, be alive. LeWitt died in 2007. The next year, more than sixty artists and students spent six months covering nearly an acre of wall in Massachusetts with a hundred and five of his drawings. He wasn't there.

title: WARM BROAD GLOW
transcript: Two words in neon. negro sunshine. Sixteen feet across. All lowercase. And the letters are black. But you can read every word. This is Glenn Ligon's first neon. He gets the words from Gertrude Stein's Three Lives, published in 1909. She's describing a Black woman named Rose. Says Rose doesn't have the "wide, abandoned laughter" that makes "the warm broad glow of negro sunshine." Like there's a laugh she's supposed to have. Years later, a young Black writer named Richard Wright finds that book in a Chicago library. Native Son is years away. Right now, he's reading a white woman and hearing his grandmother. Then he reads a left-wing critic tearing into Stein in the paper. Calls her decadent. So Wright tries something. As he later tells it, he gathers Black stockyard workers in a basement and reads them the story these two words come from. They understand every word. Slapping their thighs. Interrupting him to say where they'd met a girl like that. They recognize people. Now, a lot of Ligon's work starts with somebody else's sentences. He stencils them in black. Layering them over and over. The words get harder to read toward the bottom. And when he gets to Stein, he's clear about the stereotypes. Says she's not giving you a full picture of Black humanity. But "negro sunshine" gives him something else to work with. Black joy. In a country he describes as mostly anti-Black, he says any expression of that joy is a kind of resistance. So he takes the words out of her sentence. Warm Broad Glow becomes the title. negro sunshine goes on the wall. He leaves the cords hanging down. Transformer boxes on the floor. And the fronts of the tubes are coated in black rubber. So the light comes out behind the words. A halo around a blackout. Every letter black. Still lighting up the wall.

title: UNTITLED
transcript: So Wade Guyton makes his art on a printer. Has since 2002. This one starts in Microsoft Word. Types an X. Repeats it. Makes it bigger. Then sends the image to a big Epson inkjet printer. Except he's feeding it primed linen. The thick stuff you'd normally stretch over a wooden frame and paint on. But the printer is not happy. It drags. It slips. The ink pools. Guyton has to help it through. Coax it. Pull the fabric. Now look at the right side. Clean. Crisp edges. They showed up on time and followed the instructions. Then the left side. They bunched together. Smear. Land on top of each other. Same basic shape. A very different afternoon. And Guyton keeps those marks. That smear looks like somebody lost their temper with a brush. It came out of a printer. But he's the one who put the wrong material in there. Kept working it through. Decided the result was worth stretching onto a frame. And once it's stretched, that's it. He can't go back into it. His words: he has to live with it, smears and all. So MoMA bought it the year after he made it. Hung it in a show they called What Is Painting? Fair question. Now, one more thing. This canvas is seven feet tall. Almost six feet wide. Too wide for the printer. Look down the middle. He folded the linen in half. Printed one side. Turned it over. Printed the other. Those two halves went through separately. One mostly behaved. The other, you've seen. The printer never saw the whole painting. Neither did Guyton, until he unfolded it.

title: TROPICAL NIGHT
transcript: Looks like somebody took a notebook apart and clipped the pages to the wall. Each drawing a little bigger than a paperback. Two hundred and sixty-eight altogether. Keep an eye out for the grapes. Little bunches of them. They'll come back. Christopher Cozier is from Trinidad. He's traveling a lot, so his studio becomes wherever he can sit down. A hotel room. A friend's place. These pages are small enough to take along. And he's tried building up a series like this before. Twice. Had to sell the drawings off to support himself. Then a grant gives him enough money to hold on to the next set. So he keeps at it for years. Calls it Tropical Night. Sounds nice. Warm breeze. A drink with some fruit in it. Basically the Caribbean made for people with return tickets. That's the version he's pushing back on. The colorful, fruit-filled one. Then you get close. Little figures. Fences. Writing crowded around the images. A map keeps turning up. Bits of the world following him from room to room. And he keeps changing what goes next to what. That's why the clips matter. Every time the work goes up, he can rearrange it according to what's happening in the world. Or how he's feeling. Same drawings. New connections. Now, those grapes. Cozier borrowed them from the cover of Nelson's West Indian Readers. A schoolbook from a British publisher. First published in 1928. Generations of Caribbean children learned to read from it. Anyone who grew up with that book might know those grapes on sight. Now he's put that familiar little picture among his own drawings. His notes. His travels. What's happening around him. And every time he shows these pages, he can rearrange them. Change what goes next to what. That old schoolbook told you which page came next. Here, he gets to decide.

title: HEAD OF JAKE
transcript: It looks like it took about twenty minutes. One stroke for the mouth. A dash for an eye. A ridge of paint where the nose goes. The dark red lines do the drawing. Cheek, jaw, chin. The shoulders are one big cream sweep. Fast enough to still look wet. A head, about life-size. You can nearly count the marks. The date says 2006 to 2007. So where did a year of painting go? Auerbach painted in the same Camden studio most of his life. Went in nearly every day. And the same few people came to him. Same day, same hour, week after week. Some of them for forty years. At the end of a sitting, he'd look at what he had. If it wasn't right, he scraped it off. All of it. Down to the canvas. Next week, same person, start again. The head you're left with is the last one. The one he didn't scrape. The scrapings just piled up around the easel. Now. The sitter. Jake is his son. And when Jake was a kid, they didn't see each other at all. Twelve years. They met again in 1976. Then Jake started coming to the studio. Same day, same hour. He kept that slot for decades. Sat still while his father painted him, scraped him off, and painted him again. A year of those sittings came down to this one head. Almost none of the others survived. The appointment did.

title: COLOMBIA
transcript: Alright. Look. It’s just a word. Red. White script. The font you’ve seen before, on a can, in every deli from here to Bogotá. Your brain’s already finishing the word. Co, co… You know how this goes. Then your eye catches up. Oh. Wait. The guy is Antonio Caro. He’d done a little time in advertising. And he once showed up at the national salon with a salt bust of the president and dissolved it with water at the opening. Flooded the gallery. Then he tried a logo. Marlboro. A jury turned it down. Later, at a party, a woman says to him, you already did the Marlboro, why not do the Coca-Cola? So he does. He said it was easy. Colombia and Coca-Cola have the same number of letters. Eight. Count them. Even the big C does the swoop. That handwriting belongs to an American soda company. Trademarked. Shh. Nobody tell Coke. A poet called it a charming bit of silliness. And then one of the jurors called it real political art. Caro used to say he was stupid. And clumsy with his hands. Doubly clumsy, he said. Got one idea a year, then kept at it until everybody was tired of it. This one, he kept at for the rest of his life. He said it's the one that made him an artist. Back home, it's a classic. Now, this one was made decades later. Looks like it came out of a factory. It didn't. Two guys painted it by hand, on steel. Swoop and all.

title: EQUAL
transcript: Alright, so they put Richard Serra in a cage, hook it to a crane, and move him toward a block of white-hot steel. He's got the whole outfit on. Asbestos suit, hood, big boots, big gloves. And he's holding a tool for checking if a corner's square. That's what he's up there for. A corner. He'd asked the guys at the forge how sharp they could get the edges. They'd never done anything this big that precisely. He wanted it as tight as possible. And they said, "OK, you do it." He'd worked in steel mills as a kid. So you know... Heavy steel didn't scare him much. So, go stand at a corner of one of these blocks. He was there too. Under somewhat different conditions. That edge in front of you. That's what he wanted tight. He'd been making sculpture since the sixties, by the way. None of it was a picture of anything. Big heavy things you have to walk around. So getting you in here mattered to him. He had opinions about people getting their art through a screen. Sure, you get the look of a thing. But, the weight doesn't come through. Serra said this space seems to let you find the weight of your body against the weight of the piece. Eight blocks. Solid forged steel. Forty tons each. Almost cubes, but not totally square shaped. Bottom one's about your height. Then another one on top. If the top one's turned a different way, it hangs over, or comes up short. Each stack's turned its own way. And every stack still comes out the same height. Eleven feet. He called it Equal. Now walk around. The other stacks start moving around on you. One slides out from behind another. A gap opens. Another face appears. Same height. Same eighty tons. The steel hasn't done anything. You've just walked a few feet. He could specify every inch of the blocks. But, he couldn't stand here for you.

title: ATTICA SERIES DESK
transcript: You know this desk. Black steel. Fake-wood top. You may have seen it at a school office or a waiting room. But you've probably never wondered who made it. In 2025, Frieze magazine makes a list of the best artworks of the century so far. Puts this at number one. It was made by prisoners at the Attica Correctional Facility. Sold through Corcraft, the sales arm of New York's prison system. In the catalog, it's called the Attica Series. That's Corcraft's name for it. The same Attica where, in 1971, nearly thirteen hundred prisoners take control of the yard. A twenty-one-year-old named L. D. Barkley reads their statement to the news cameras. "We are men. We are not beasts." Among their demands, they want the state minimum wage for the work they do inside. And on their list, in capital letters: "STOP SLAVE LABOR." Four days later, the state retakes the prison. Helicopters. Tear gas. Gunfire. Thirty-nine people die in the retaking. Prisoners and hostages. All killed by gunfire from the state's forces. Barkley is one of them. He was just days away from getting out. So now it's 2016. An artist named Cameron Rowland gets this desk, changes nothing, and puts it in a show at Artists Space in New York. In the exhibition text, Rowland gives the pay range for people working in New York prisons. Ten cents to a dollar fourteen an hour. And getting the desk into the gallery takes some paperwork. Corcraft won't sell to an individual, but it does sell to certain nonprofits. And the gallery somehow qualifies. So the gallery registers as a customer. Its customer number becomes the name of the show. Later, the desk comes here to MoMA. But Rowland won't sell it. MoMA has to rent it. Five years at a time. And that whole five-year rental costs what the desk originally cost in the prison catalog. MoMA can show it. Has to look after it. Can't buy it. Now, the essay Rowland wrote for that first gallery show, it opens with the Thirteenth Amendment. The one that abolished slavery. There's an exception in it, which states: "Except as a punishment for crime."

title: BEING HUMAN
transcript: Sooner or later, Taylor Swift shows up on that glass. But it's not her. Close, though. She's sitting in a cane chair. Hotel bed behind her. A stone Buddha head on a little table. A computer put her together from interviews it found online. And she's projected onto glass. You can see the room right through her. Keep an eye on that room. Christopher Kulendran Thomas made this with Annika Kuhlmann. It's called Being Human. Then the film puts you on a train. A young Tamil artist is talking about Kant. Human rights. He's real. Sri Lanka's civil war lasted twenty-six years. It ended with a massacre of Tamil civilians. Kulendran Thomas grew up in London. His family is Tamil. They'd left Sri Lanka as the violence got worse. And around the time the war ended, something else was getting started in Colombo. An art market. A biennale. New galleries. People buying. Now, Kulendran Thomas has a problem with how this works. He says artists like him get rewarded for performing where they're from. Make something that looks like what the buyer thinks Sri Lanka looks like. The postcard version. Then he goes shopping. Five paintings and sculptures by Sri Lankan artists. All from one gallery in Colombo. Two are by Kingsley Gunatillake. Then he adds another. Looks like a Gunatillake. Gunatillake didn't make it. Kulendran Thomas did, using a computer trained on work by Sri Lankan artists. And he puts it in the room with the others. The room you've been looking at through Taylor Swift. Six works. One didn't come from the gallery. Go on. See if you can tell. And the thing they've given the fake Taylor Swift to talk about? Being real.

title: ARK
transcript: Eighteen feet across. Almost twelve feet tall. Not one piece of it standing up straight. For about fifty years, Joel Shapiro made people. Little blocky figures. Arms and legs out of rectangular beams, caught mid-stride or mid-fall. He made a person out of four blocks and made you believe it. That little switch your brain makes. One second, a person. The next, just a bunch of wood stuck together. Now count the people in this one. There aren't any. But the switch keeps happening. You keep waiting for these slabs to turn into a body. They never quite do. Red, mostly. One blue. A grey one cutting down through the middle. And a yellow blade going up, higher than everything else. One part shoves. Another braces. Another throws its weight out over the floor. The empty space is carrying as much as the wood is. Nothing in here is resting. And the color isn't paint, exactly. It's casein. Milk protein. It dries dead matte. He finished this one in 2024. He died the following June, at eighty-three. He called it ARK. The boat you build when you can see what's coming. Except this one doesn't look built to float. It looks caught in the second before everything hits the floor. But nothing does. All that weight. All those directions. Still holding.

title: INGENIO
transcript: At first glance, this looks like a huge rusted wok. Or something a guy in Brooklyn swears he's gonna turn into a fire pit. It's a sugar kettle. Nineteenth century. Cast iron. Made in England, used in Louisiana. Sixteen hundred pounds. Look at that crack down the side. From the rim down into the belly. Cameron Rowland calls this Ingenio. That's what a colonial sugar mill was called in Spanish. The engine. And this was one of its parts. Once you cut sugarcane, it starts going bad. You've got to process it fast. So the mill runs sixteen, eighteen hours a day. Enslaved Black people grow the cane, cut it, crush it, then boil the juice in a bunch of kettles like this one. All that work. So Rowland writes the caption for this. It tells you all of that. And how the work was enforced. It quotes this historian, C. L. R. James. James describes enslaved people getting the whip more reliably than they got their food. Then comes the last line. "Sugar was made this way for four hundred years." Sugar has incredible PR. Think about it. Sugar is cupcakes. Your aunt asking if you want one lump or two. But you definitely don't picture this thing. Or the people made to work around it. Now, here's how Rowland ended up with it. While doing research, Rowland comes across a business outside Atlanta selling old sugar kettles. For people's gardens. Fountains. Fire pits. On the website, some of the owners pose beside them in their yards. So Rowland buys this one. Out of that trade. Same kettle. Different caption.
